text: Thank you, Ellie. Hello, everyone.
It is a great honor to be speaking in this beautiful room at TADWIG in what is an
incredibly significant year for the Biodiversity Heritage Library.
Those of you who have been following along will know that we have been on a
precarious and uncertain journey.
Last year, we were thrown into the wilderness, and we have had to find our own way
out. This beautiful illustration is from Joseph Hooker's 1854 Himalayan
journals. It's a living bridge. It is formed from the aerial roots of fig trees,
and for me, it really captures where BHL is right now.
For the past 18 months, we've been building a new bridge for BHL.
It is holding us up for now. We've put down some strong roots, but there are gaps.
BHL could still fall, and we don't yet know what is on the other side, which is
both scary and exciting. Today, I'm going to tell you the story of how we've got
this far and what it still might take to get to the other side.
Now, I know most in the room are very familiar with BHL because it is essential to
your work. But for those who aren't, the Biodiversity Heritage Library is the
world's largest virtual library of open access biodiversity literature and archival
material, and one of the world's most critical resources of biodiversity knowledge.
It is a global consortium of 684 contributing organizations and libraries who have
together made over 64 million pages of biodiversity knowledge freely accessible
online. It contains information on millions of the world's species and is the
foundation of our understanding of biodiversity.
BHL exists because the cultivation of natural science cannot be efficiently carried
on without reference to an extensive library, and the extensive library on BHL
contains information and resources produced as early as the 1100s and as recently
as last month.
Every page is fully searchable. Our taxonomic name recognition allows you to search
for both current and past scientific names.
We have added article data to over 450 scientific articles, and over 80,000
of those now have DOIs, bringing those articles into the modern linked network of
scholarly research. We retrospectively assign DOIs to species descriptions
published centuries ago, all the way through to the current day.
This is a DOI BHL assigned to a species description that was published in November
last year. To give you a sense of the massive amount of information made accessible
and discoverable on the Biodiversity Heritage Library, this is a map produced by
Rod Page. Every single dot on this map represents a latitude and a longitude pair
in a scholarly article on BHL.
However, this important discoverability work and our work assigning DOIs and many
other BHL projects were put on hold last year when we were thrown into an emergency
mode, when we received the unexpected news that the Smithsonian Institution, our
administrative and technical home, would cease to host the BHL on the 1st of
January this year. This decision placed BHL, one of the world's most widely used
and longest-running biodiversity infrastructures, at risk.
We were completely at sea, with the very real possibility of being pulled under.
As our host, the Smithsonian had provided the BHL secretariat staff and the
technical team, as well as the seven servers required to run the BHL website and
the website itself. With this support gone, we had to act quickly if we were to
help keep BHL afloat. We formed an emergency and transition team, and together with
the BHL Executive Committee, we have worked tirelessly over the past 18 months to
build a more autonomous, global, and sustainable BHL.
At this point, back in April last year, we had no idea what we were going to do,
how we would gather the support we needed to continue, or what the future of BHL
might look like. So it was more important than ever for us to communicate openly
and honestly with our community, to say that we didn't yet know what we were going
to do, we didn't have the answers, to invite their ideas and support, and to
reassure them that we would do everything we could to save the BHL and its staff.
We communicated every stage of the transition across our blog and on social media,
and we started a community forum on Discourse to invite their ideas and concerns.
The threat to the BHL encouraged an overwhelming outpouring of appreciation
and panic from our users. These included comments like, "BHL is one of the most
important, most valuable online projects and one of the greatest collections on the
internet. It is an indispensable record of the earth's biodiversity and represents
an invaluable part of our scientific and cultural heritage.
It's an absolutely vital resource for ecologists and evolutionary biologists." This
was my favorite, a pledge from a user.
She says, "I will send a box of handmade cookies every year for the rest of my life
to whichever institution takes on the BHL."
In June last year, we opened a global call for support, inviting expressions of
interest from institutions and stakeholders to host BHL's operational and technical
roles and services. In August, we moved to a new financial and legal home, the
Council on Library and Information Resources.
This means that BHL is now independently able to accept donations, pursue grants,
and manage our own staff contracts. It also provide BHL with autonomy.
BHL is no longer constrained by a single US federally affiliated
university, no longer constrained by their requirements and shifting priorities.
We're now operating as an independent, globally governed consortium.
BHL's call for support invited offers of technical hosting,
support for our existing systems, and some start funding.
What we received is giving us stability for one to two years.
I want to really emphasize this. BHL is secure and only secure
through to 2027.
On the 1st of January, BHL officially moved across to its new independent chapter.
On the left is our blog post explaining what that means for BHL and its staff, and
in February, we shared the exciting news that we have secured the staff positions
of all existing staff.
During this time, we have been extremely grateful to our BHL members.
These are the organizations who govern BHL and whose membership fees, along with
those of our affiliates, provide BHL with a reliable source of support.
Three of those organizations, the University of South Florida, Vanderbilt
University, and Zenberg Nature Support, joined BHL during the transition.
At the most uncertain time in BHL's history, these organizations decided that we
were worth supporting and joining.
Two of those organizations are providing BHL with significant technical support.
The University of South Florida Libraries are providing significant system support
from the core,
BHL's metadata collection workflow system, for three years, while Vanderbilt
University is providing us with an associate cloud engineer.
Rahul Sharma joins the technical team in BHL in February, and his role will help
build a resilient modern technical foundation for BHL.
But the news that most excited our users was that the Field Museum would take over
the hosting of BHL's website and technical infrastructure.
This was the news that answered the question that was most asked by our users
during the transition, which was, what is going to happen to the BHL website?
The response was an outpouring of relief and gratitude from across the world.
It was the best news. That the incredible free, open treasure trove of nature and
the crown jewel of biodiversity literature had been saved.
And from my favorite user, "I now know where to send cookies."
That big move from Washington, DC, to Chicago was completed at the end of June and
marked the final piece of our transition away from the Smithsonian.
With BHL's immediate future becoming more stable, we were finally able to start
thinking beyond survival to the future of BHL's aging platform.
Critical part of this process was to ask our users what they most wanted improved.
In July, we ran a BHL user survey, and the message was clear.
Enhanced text search was our users' number one priority, followed by image search
and an improved page viewer.
Our BHL platform modernization project is now underway, and it's much more than a
technical upgrade. The goal is to replace BHL's legacy infrastructure with a modern
cloud-based platform that has better search and discovery, improved performance and
reliability, and data that is connected, machine actionable, and easier to find,
reuse, and connect through better APIs, linked data, and persistent identifiers.
Alongside this work, we have some really exciting new collaborations underway,
including a major project led by the Natural History Museum in London.
The NHM team is developing new ways to unlock biodiversity literature at scale, and
they're in the final stages of recruiting a data scientist dedicated to this
project. Here is who will be speaking more about this exciting work tomorrow in our
BHL symposium. Encourage you to come along.
We've also expanded the BHL executive committee, adding a strategic development
officer and a member at large, which will increase our capacity for fundraising,
partnerships, and long-term planning.
David Eagleman, our chair, and our new strategic development officer, Amanda Bozar,
are both here at tADWIG this week. Please do go and talk to them.
Building this new future has also made us realize that BHL needs a more diverse and
resilient funding base. At the end of 2025, we ran a targeted campaign called Give
BHL Wings, calling on our users to help BHL take flight by the 1st of January.
We set a target of $50,000 US, and we reached that goal on New Year's Eve, which
totally made my year.
Our plea also reached the media. In June this year, The Guardian published a major
feature on BHL, bringing BHL and the very real threat to its future to a much wider
audience. We saw an immediate spike in our public donations, which brought in more
than $10,000 US on the day that article was published.
We were blown away by messages of support and calls to save the extraordinary BHL.
One reader suggested that if you're a tech billionaire or even just a millionaire,
you could do something extraordinary.
So if you do know one, please send them our way.
BHL had never had to rely on public fundraising before this.
Now we do, and the response has been amazing.
Last week, just in time for tADWIG, our online public donations reached $100,000
US, more than 1,750 individual donations from 48 countries,
demonstrating how deeply individuals value BHL.
This includes more than $2,200 US per month in recurring donations.
Our current campaign, Become a BHL Sustainer, is trying to increase that reliable
ongoing support. If you can afford a cup of coffee every week, please do join our
BHL Sustains program.
2026 does not only mark the beginning of BHL's new chapter, it is also BHL's 20th
anniversary. Happy birthday, BHL.
One of the ways we're celebrating this huge milestone is by showcasing the
extraordinary breadth and history of BHL's collections and the people and the
institutions that make BHL possible.
Each post in this series celebrates the incredible treasures.
Each one has been selected by a member of our community.
So of course, they include rare books and historic field diaries.
But they also showcase the treasure between the covers, such as the article data
that makes our species descriptions discoverable.
And our most recent post celebrates BHL as a repository of information about
extinct species. I encourage you to check them out and follow along as our series
unfolds through our anniversary year.
We've come a long way across this bridge.
Last year, there were times when we genuinely did not know if BHL would have a
future. Today, we have a new foundation beneath us, new partnerships, new
possibilities, new funding streams, new grants in the pipeline, and an
extraordinary network of people and organizations holding us up.
But I cannot stand here in front of you and say that BHL's future is secure.
It isn't. We need to stop taking BHL for granted.
A living bridge becomes stronger as more roots reach out, grow, intertwine, and
together strengthen the whole. BHL now has the independence and autonomy to welcome
ideas, partnerships, collaboration, and possibilities.
So if you or your organization has expertise, resources, funding, or connections
that could help make BHL stronger, please do reach out.
BHL's future is not yet fixed, and that's what makes this time so exciting.
We will be exploring BHL's future opportunities and possibilities throughout this
week at tADWIG. Tomorrow afternoon, we have two back-to-back sessions and a
dedicated BHL symposium where we'll explore some of those new partnerships,
infrastructure, and ideas that are already reimagining and transforming BHL.
And on Thursday, we have a hands-on workshop where we'll be exploring new
approaches and tools to maximize the value of the Biodiversity Heritage Library.
We invite you to join and help build VHL's future. Thank you for listening.
We do have a minute for a question, if anyone has one.
Or you can come and find Nicole later.
Or come to our symposium or our workshop. I'll be there.
